references.text: Jacob dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down on it – the background for his awe-filled exclamation that the place is God's house and the gate of heaven.

Jacob builds an altar at the place and calls it El-Betel ('God of Bethel'), because God revealed Himself to him there – a direct follow-up to his recognition of the place as 'the house of God' in 28:17.
Moses at the burning bush is told that the ground where he stands is holy, paralleling Jacob's experience of a place that inspired awe because God was there.
The psalmist's longing for the Lord's dwellings and His courts reflects Jacob's recognition of the place as God's house and the gate of heaven.
Jesus says the disciples will see heaven opened and God's angels ascending and descending over the Son of Man – a direct allusion to Jacob's dream and the gate of heaven.
Christ entered into heaven itself to appear before God's face on our behalf, pointing toward the heavenly reality behind Jacob's vision of the gate of heaven.
Believers are described as living stones being built up into a spiritual house, an expansion of the idea of God's house that Jacob recognized at Bethel.
Theological contrast: Jacob's awe for 'the house of God' stands in sharp opposition to the beast's mockery of God's dwelling place.
Thematic parallel: Humanity's response to the Lord's house – either as a place of God's presence (Bethel) or as evidence of God's judgment (the destroyed temple).
Contrast at the entrance to the sanctuary: Ezekiel's idol image (false) versus Jacob's revelation of God's house (true).
Thematic contrast: Jacob's discovery of 'the Lord's house' as holy versus Jeremiah's lament that foreigners have entered that same house.
